extracted.intended_audience: administrative law scholars, regulators, practitioners, and policy makers interested in self-regulatory organizations (SROs) and notice-and-comment rulemaking
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluate and analyze statutory, procedural, and practical rules governing self-regulatory organizations (SROs) and the oversight agencies (e.g., SEC, CFTC, FERC, NERC), including rulemaking, enforcement, transparency, and standards of judicial review.

rubrics_metrics.name: SEC review of SRO rules and orders (de novo authority)
rubrics_metrics.description: The SEC reviews FINRA orders de novo and has authority to affirm, modify, set aside, or remand an SRO’s sanction (15 U.S.C. §§78s(d)–(e)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although statutory language contemplates de novo review, in practice the SEC almost always approves SRO rules and often engages in negotiation with FINRA; the article highlights a gap between the formal de novo authority and practical deference. See Charles Schwab, 861 F. Supp. 2d at 1066 for review procedures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comptroller General (GAO) triennial report requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Dodd‑Frank requires the Comptroller General (GAO) to submit a detailed report to Congress every three years evaluating the SEC’s oversight of FINRA (15 U.S.C. §78d‑9).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The GAO studies have documented limited SEC review of governance matters (e.g., executive compensation), infrequent disapprovals, and lack of formal processes to evaluate the effectiveness of existing SRO rules—evidence used to assess oversight effectiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: SEC independent consultant and biannual reporting (Dodd‑Frank §967)
rubrics_metrics.description: Dodd‑Frank requires the SEC to hire an independent consultant “of high caliber and with expertise” to examine SEC relationships with SROs and to provide reports to Congress every six months for two years describing responses to the consultant’s recommendations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The consultant’s report generally recommended strengthening SEC oversight, improving coordination, and strengthening processes for SRO rule proposals; the SEC’s follow-up reports documented some improvements (e.g., electronic records, rule dashboards).

rubrics_metrics.name: SEC statutory limits on ensuring cross-market rule consistency
rubrics_metrics.description: The SEC lacks statutory authority effectively to ensure consistency of rules across markets; SRO rules can conflict yet still comply with the Exchange Act.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This statutory limitation constrains oversight agencies’ ability to harmonize SRO rules and is a structural factor when evaluating oversight effectiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presumption of effectiveness due to agency inaction / statutory timing rules
rubrics_metrics.description: In several SRO schemes (e.g., SEC, CFTC/NFA), proposed rules can become effective—binding law—if the oversight agency fails to meet statutory review deadlines (e.g., NFA may make rules effective ten days after submission; similar SEC timing consequences exist).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This timing presumption places the burden of inertia on the agency, creating a practical presumption of validity for SRO proposals and reducing the incentive for thorough agency review.

rubrics_metrics.name: FINRA–SEC negotiated review practice
rubrics_metrics.description: FINRA responds to comments and negotiates with the SEC during the rule review process; the agency almost always approves rules and rarely uses its authority to modify them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The appearance of APA-style notice-and-comment is disrupted by behind-the-scenes negotiation and industry influence; comments on complex rules tend to come predominantly from regulated industry, skewing outcomes in industry’s favor.

rubrics_metrics.name: CFTC/NFA ten‑day presumption and review windows
rubrics_metrics.description: When the NFA submits rules to the CFTC, the NFA “may make such rules effective ten days after receipt of such submission,” but the CFTC may decide to review the rules, triggering a notice-and-hearing period and extending the review time (7 U.S.C. §21(j)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although the statute permits extended review (e.g., up to 180 days or up to one year), in practice the CFTC rarely finds problems; studies show NFA rules went into effect without CFTC intervention nearly 100% of the time.

rubrics_metrics.name: CFTC standard of review for NFA adjudications: weight of the evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: The CFTC has interpreted its statute to require use of the more deferential 'weight of the evidence' standard when reviewing NFA adjudications (see MBH Commodity Advisors, 250 F.3d at 1060–63; 17 C.F.R. §171.34).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts (e.g., Seventh Circuit) upheld the deferential approach reasoning that appellate de novo review would ignore the SRO’s industry expertise; this is an example where statutory/regulatory interpretation leads to administrative deference in enforcement review.

rubrics_metrics.name: CFTC powers to abrogate/alter and to reduce penalties
rubrics_metrics.description: The CFTC can abrogate and request alterations to futures-association rules (7 U.S.C. §21(k)) and can reduce any penalty if it finds the penalty is 'excessive or oppressive' (7 U.S.C. §21(i)(2)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are statutory tools for oversight, but the article notes they are seldom exercised in practice, limiting their practical impact as corrective mechanisms.

rubrics_metrics.name: NERC governance rule requirements (EPAct of 2005)
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the Energy Policy Act of 2005, NERC must establish rules of governance that 'provide for reasonable notice and opportunity for public comment, due process, openness, and balancing of interests in developing reliability standards' (16 U.S.C. §824o(c)(2)(D)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These governance requirements are statutory benchmarks used to evaluate whether NERC’s internal processes meet minimal public‑interest and due‑process expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: ANSI consensus‑based standards process features
rubrics_metrics.description: NERC’s reliability standards are developed through a hybrid process drawing from FERC requirements and the ANSI consensus development process: standards committees develop scope/purpose, appoint drafting teams, post drafts for comment, oversee field testing, incorporate revisions, and submit to a broad 'ballot body' vote.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The ANSI features (participation, formal voting, field testing) afford structured stakeholder involvement, but they do not create an administrative record suitable for judicial review and can be slow and industry-dominated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ballot body composition and weighted voting (NERC)
rubrics_metrics.description: The ballot body includes utilities, markets, generators, purchasers, citizen/consumer groups, and state commissions; however, consumer groups are few and votes are weighted (e.g., consumers 30% weight vs generators full weight), producing sectoral imbalances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Weighted voting and uneven sector representation dilute public-interest voices and can be used to evaluate fairness and balance of the standards-development process.

rubrics_metrics.name: NERC Board approval constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: After the ballot, which must pass by sixty percent, NERC’s Board of Trustees votes on the proposal; the Board may approve or reject a standard but may not modify it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This restriction limits corrective action by the Board and creates an inflexible pass/reject dynamic that may contribute to inefficiencies and standoffs with FERC.

rubrics_metrics.name: FERC substantive standard and 'due weight' to NERC expertise
rubrics_metrics.description: FERC must consider whether proposed reliability standards are 'just, reasonable, not unduly discriminatory or preferential, and in the public interest,' but must 'give due weight to the technical expertise' of NERC on matters other than competition (16 U.S.C. §824o(d)(2)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statutorily mandated deference to NERC’s technical judgments introduces ambiguity for FERC in balancing deference with its independent public‑interest mandate; commentators note confusion about how to implement 'due weight.'

rubrics_metrics.name: FERC remand-only authority (cannot redraft standards)
rubrics_metrics.description: If FERC disapproves a proposed rule, it must remand the matter to NERC and lacks authority to redraft standards or create new ones (16 U.S.C. §824o(d)(4)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This limitation leads to iterative back-and-forth between FERC and NERC, producing inefficiency and delay and limiting FERC’s capacity to craft alternative regulatory text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Absence of APA-style administrative record in ANSI process
rubrics_metrics.description: The ANSI process used by NERC is not suited for creating an administrative record akin to an APA administrative-rulemaking record (contrast 5 U.S.C. §553(c), which requires a concise statement of basis and purpose).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The lack of a robust administrative record impedes judicial review and obscures decision rationales, reducing transparency and accountability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standards‑development time delays
rubrics_metrics.description: NERC’s standards-development process is lengthy—development reportedly takes over three years on average and sometimes over five years.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Significant delay is an efficiency concern and a metric when assessing whether a standards-development regime meets statutory goals of timely reliability improvements.

rubrics_metrics.name: NERC enforcement procedures and closed hearings
rubrics_metrics.description: NERC’s hearing procedures provide for an initial notice of violation followed by a hearing before a hearing officer; the hearing is closed to the public; a hearing panel may issue a final order, which is appealable to NERC, and thereafter an aggrieved party may seek FERC review (NERC procedures; 16 U.S.C. §824o(e)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Closed hearings and multi‑tier internal appeals raise transparency concerns and affect the public’s ability to monitor enforcement processes; however, notices of penalty and enforcement actions are made public by NERC.

rubrics_metrics.name: FERC’s enforcement authority vs review standard ambiguity
rubrics_metrics.description: The statute does not specify the standard of review for FERC’s review of NERC enforcement, but it permits FERC broader authority than in its review of rules (e.g., modify penalty; take action against NERC to ensure compliance) (16 U.S.C. §824o(e)(5)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Early practice shows FERC often leaves enforcement to NERC but steps in for high‑profile incidents; the undefined review standard creates uncertainty about the scope of FERC oversight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Opacity of certain SRO rulemaking processes (e.g., NFA)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some SROs (e.g., NFA) provide little public description of their internal rulemaking procedures (no description on NFA website or in manual/bylaws), making it difficult to identify how rules are developed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Opacity hinders descriptive and normative evaluation of SRO processes and suggests reliance on informal/back‑channel bargaining that cannot be externally assessed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Oversight agencies’ lack of formal processes to evaluate existing rules
rubrics_metrics.description: The SEC (and other oversight agencies) lack formal processes for evaluating the effectiveness of existing SRO rules (GAO finding).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Absence of ex post evaluation procedures is a criterion for assessing oversight robustness and contributes to regulatory inertia and persistent deference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Participation limitations and stakeholder imbalance
rubrics_metrics.description: Participation in SRO rulemaking is not open to all 'interested persons' but to a defined set of industry members and registered stakeholders; public-interest actors are outnumbered and sometimes underweighted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate SRO processes by measuring who is permitted to participate, the relative number of participants from each sector, vote weighting, and whether public-interest voices are effectively diluted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicial reviewability doctrines as barriers (finality, ripeness, exhaustion, standing, zone of interests)
rubrics_metrics.description: Doctrines such as finality, ripeness, exhaustion, standing, and zone of interests may prevent certain petitioners or agency behaviors from entering the judicial forum, potentially compounding obstacles posed by SRO processes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing the availability of judicial review, analyze whether these doctrines operate differently in SRO contexts and whether SRO stakeholder processes produce waiver or exhaustion problems (e.g., FERC requires showing how concerns were presented to the SRO).

rubrics_metrics.name: Courts’ tendency to analogize SRO procedures to APA procedures
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts have been willing to analogize the procedural constraints governing SROs to agency procedures under the Administrative Procedure Act (APA), treating some SRO processes as if they were APA rulemakings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This analogy may be convenient but risks ignoring material differences (industry composition, voting procedures, lack of administrative record) between SROs and federal agencies and should be scrutinized in evaluations of judicial handling of SRO decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory and practical embedding of deference in SRO schemes
rubrics_metrics.description: Deference to SROs is built into statutory schemes explicitly (e.g., 'give due weight') or practically (e.g., agencies rarely disapprove rules), producing limited oversight in practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assessors should examine both explicit statutory provisions and empirical evidence of agency behavior to determine the degree and consequences of deference in particular SRO regimes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Settlement bias in enforcement outcomes
rubrics_metrics.description: Most SRO enforcement matters (e.g., NERC reliability violations) tend to settle, and oversight agencies often decline to review the bulk of notices of proposed violations (FERC example declined to review nearly 1,000 violations in a fiscal year).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: High settlement rates and limited agency review reduce transparency and judicially reviewable determinations; use settlement prevalence as an indicator of enforcement transparency and oversight intensity.
